standard.title: Addition and subtraction with place value
standard.description: add and subtract two- and three-digit numbers using place value to partition, rearrange and regroup numbers to assist in calculations without a calculator
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can add and subtract one- and two-digit numbers using part-part-whole reasoning and a variety of calculation strategies (AC9M2N04). They have not yet applied place value partitioning and regrouping to three-digit calculations without a calculator.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students add and subtract two- and three-digit numbers, applying place value partitioning, rearranging and regrouping strategies to calculate without a calculator.

nodes.label: Partitioning for addition
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can partition two- and three-digit numbers to add by place value (e.g. 245 + 132 = 200+100 + 40+30 + 5+2).
nodes.minimum_width: Add at least two pairs of three-digit numbers by partitioning into hundreds, tens and ones, recording the working.
nodes.typical_width: Apply place value partitioning to add a range of two- and three-digit number pairs; connect to informal written layout.
wider: Explore different partitioning strategies — e.g. partitioning one number only, or using non-standard partitions like 245 = 200+45
Apply partitioning addition to multi-step problems and real-world contexts involving distances or quantities
success_criteria: Students can partition both addends by place value and combine to find the sum.
Students can record the partitioned addition strategy clearly.

nodes.label: Regrouping in addition
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise when regrouping (carrying) is needed in addition and apply it correctly across hundreds, tens and ones.
nodes.minimum_width: Solve at least three addition problems requiring at least one regrouping step, explaining where the regrouping occurs.
nodes.typical_width: Add two- and three-digit numbers across a range of problems requiring regrouping at tens and/or hundreds; explain the regrouping action using place value language.
wider: Use base-ten blocks or virtual manipulatives to model the physical exchange that underlies regrouping, connecting the model to the written procedure
Investigate what happens when regrouping is needed at multiple places simultaneously

response_modes.reason: Regrouping is a common error site — students who see it only in columns of the same type (tens only) often fail to generalise. Encountering it at hundreds, tens and ones across varied problems resolves the confusion.

nodes.hinge_reason: Regrouping in addition is a prerequisite for decomposition in Node 3 subtraction — students who have not generalised regrouping across place value positions cannot reliably apply the inverse procedure (decomposition/borrowing) and will produce systematic errors in subtraction.
success_criteria: Students can identify when regrouping is needed in an addition calculation.
Students can correctly apply regrouping and produce the correct sum.

nodes.label: Subtraction using place value
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can subtract two- and three-digit numbers using place value partitioning, including cases requiring decomposition.
nodes.minimum_width: Subtract two pairs of three-digit numbers using place value partitioning; at least one problem requires decomposition (borrowing).
nodes.typical_width: Apply place value strategies — partitioning, rearranging, decomposition — to subtract across a range of two- and three-digit problems; choose the most efficient strategy.
wider: Compare different subtraction strategies (partitioning, counting on/back, compensation) for the same problem, evaluating efficiency
Apply subtraction to financial contexts — e.g. calculating change from $100 in real-world purchase scenarios

response_modes.reason: Subtraction with decomposition is the highest-error node in this descriptor — the 'borrowing' action is procedurally error-prone. Students who understand the place value rationale through multiple representations (models and written) make fewer errors than those who memorise procedure.
Once the decomposition concept is understood, students also benefit from practice to build fluency and reduce procedural errors in multi-step problems.

nodes.hinge_reason: Subtraction with decomposition feeds directly into AC9M3N06 mathematical modelling problems and AC9M3N05 estimation-checking tasks — students who cannot reliably subtract with decomposition cannot complete multi-step problems or check the reasonableness of results in subsequent standards.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Strategy comparison tasks — comparing partitioning vs compensation vs counting on for the same problem — give advancing students genuine structural insight into why different strategies work and when to choose them.
success_criteria: Students can subtract a three-digit number from a three-digit number using at least one place value strategy.
Students can correctly apply decomposition where required and produce the correct difference.
